explanations: luna: The section connects هدى with a gift; here God promises guidance from Him and says whoever follows هداي will have no fear, presenting guidance as a granted path with a response.
terra: Israel is commanded to remember the favor God bestowed and to fulfill its covenant, making received niʿma answerable in memory and conduct.
terra: The repeated command to remember God’s favor addresses a people collectively, a communal counterpart to telling of one’s Lord’s favor.
terra: Israel’s covenant joins good treatment of orphans and the needy with speaking good to people, bringing the beneficent hand and tongue into the same command.
terra: The command to remember the favor is repeated at the close of the Israel passage, showing that divine gifts remain claims on the recipient’s speech and conduct.

luna: The section's gift and asker meet in the definition of righteousness: a person gives wealth from love to relatives, orphans, needy people, travelers, and السائلين. | terra: True piety includes giving loved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, askers, and captives; both orphan and open-palmed asker stand before the same giving hand.

luna: The section's سâ'il asks a human not to rebuke him; here people ask the Prophet about God, who answers that He is near and responds to the caller, distinguishing a divine answer from a human's duty to give.
luna: The section names improper reaching for another's due; this ayah forbids consuming people's wealth wrongfully or using it to influence judges.

luna: Asked what to spend, the answer names خير and directs it to parents, kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers; the section's “gift” sense of خير meets actual giving to recipients. | terra: A question about what to give is answered with whatever khayr is spent for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler; asking, gift-as-good, and the protected recipients meet directly.
terra: When people ask what to spend, the answer is “the surplus” (ٱلْعَفْوَ), turning the second sense of سؤال into a measure for the giving hand.

luna: The section forbids overpowering the orphan; this answer to a question about orphans says reforming their affairs is better and calls them brothers, shifting the hand from taking to care. | terra: A question about orphans is answered with reform as best and with guarded permission to mix affairs, showing that proximity to orphan property must serve rather than overpower them.
luna: The section's unauthorized hand reaches for another's property; this ayah forbids taking back what was given to wives, with the stated exception of an agreed ransom when the limits are feared.
terra: Believers are commanded to remember God’s favor upon them together with the revealed Book and wisdom, a close counterpart to speaking of the Lord’s niʿma.

luna: The section's transfer of a gift has a reciprocal form here: whoever lends God a goodly loan will have it multiplied many times, so giving is pictured as entrusted value returned by God. | terra: A good loan to God is received and returned many times over while God constricts and expands, turning giving into an exchange whose increase comes from above.
luna: Believers are told to spend from what God provided before a day with no buying, friendship, or intercession; it makes present giving a response to provision before the Hereafter's reckoning.
luna: The section's gift is a transfer whose reach can grow; this parable makes money spent in God's path like a grain multiplied into many ears, showing divine increase after giving.

luna: The section moves from God's gift to speaking of it; this ayah says not to follow a charitable gift with reminders or injury, guarding the recipient from a hurtful word. | terra: Those who spend must not follow what their hands give with reminder or injury, setting a boundary between recounting God’s favor and boasting of one’s own favor.

luna: This neighbor says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury, making speech to a requester part of giving well. | terra: A fitting word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by hurt; speech can honor the receiving hand when a material gift does not.

luna: It warns that charity is voided by reminders and injury; the section's report of God's gift is thus distinct from using one's gift to shame its recipient. | terra: Charity is nullified by reminders and injury, like a bare rock whose soil is stripped by rain; the transferred object cannot excuse domination of the recipient.

luna: The section's hand carries a gift to another; this command says to spend from good things earned and grown, not to choose bad goods one would not accept oneself. | terra: Givers must spend from good things and not select what they themselves would accept only with closed eyes, forcing the donor to imagine the receiving hand.
terra: Beside commands to spend, Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty, exposing the rival promises that make a hand close or open.

luna: This ayah weighs making charity visible against concealing it and giving to the poor; it complicates the section's public telling of God's favor with a distinction about human alms. | terra: Giving charity secretly to the poor is called better than public disclosure, adding a hidden transfer to the section’s gift that later becomes spoken.

luna: The section's خير can name a gift; this ayah says whatever good people spend is for themselves and will be repaid, joining خير to material giving. | terra: Whatever good believers spend returns fully to them, while guidance remains God’s affair; giving, return, and guidance are distinguished but held together.

luna: This ayah names poor people who do not ask others persistently (لا يسألون الناس إلحافا); it lets the reader see the needy who may not appear as the section's audible sâ'il. | terra: Restrained needy people are mistaken for self-sufficient because they do not ask insistently, making visible the deprived hand that never opens and still has a claim.

luna: This neighbor gives the secret/public dimension of spending: believers give by night and day, privately and openly, and have their reward with their Lord. | terra: Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, keep the giving hand active across every visible and hidden condition.

luna: The section pictures the giving hand; this ayah says خير is in God's hand and He gives and takes away sovereignty, joining bounty to God's power to grant or remove. | terra: God gives and removes sovereignty, raises and lowers, while “good is in Your hand” (بِيَدِكَ ٱلْخَيْرُ); one verse gathers the section’s divine hand, gift-as-khayr, giving, and taking from above.

luna: The section pictures the Lord's hand as giver; this ayah says bounty is بيد الله and He gives it to whom He wills, locating both the gift and its choice with God. | terra: All bounty is said to be in God’s hand, and He gives it to whom He wills; the metaphorical giver named by the section is made explicit.

luna: The section's gift is a form of خير; this ayah says righteousness is not reached until one spends from what one loves, then calls whatever is spent خير. | terra: People do not attain full piety until they give from what they love, giving Quranic form to the dictionary’s gift carried as an act of birr.
terra: The command to remember God’s favor identifies former enemies whose hearts He joined, turning an unseen divine gift into a narrated social transformation.

luna: The section warns against a closed hand; this ayah condemns those who withhold what God gave them (بما آتاهم الله من فضله), saying it will become a collar around their necks. | terra: Those who withhold what God gave them from His bounty will wear the withheld thing as a collar, turning the closed hand into the very bond around the neck evoked by 17:29.

luna: The section forbids taking from the orphan; this command says to give orphans their property and not consume it with one's own, setting the exact boundary on the hand. | terra: The command to hand orphans their property and not consume it with one’s own property directly reverses the overpowering hand that takes without the orphan’s consent.
luna: This command says to give women their bridal gifts graciously (نحلة); it makes a hand-to-hand transfer depend on honoring the recipient.
terra: Guardians must provide and clothe dependants from protected property and speak fitting words, another joining of responsible provision with honorable speech.

luna: The section's forbidden reach over the orphan is answered by testing orphans until maturity and handing their property back (فادفعوا إليهم أموالهم), rather than consuming it first. | terra: Guardians must test orphans, hand over their property at maturity, avoid consuming it wastefully, and take witnesses; it measures precisely when the upper hand must open and withdraw.

luna: When orphans, kin, and poor people are present at inheritance division, this command says to give them something and speak kindly; it joins the section's hand-gift to its concern with words. | terra: When orphans and needy people attend an estate division, the heirs must provide for them from it and speak fitting words, pairing the giving hand with the speaking mouth.

luna: The section forbids the hand that takes from an orphan without consent; this ayah says those who consume orphans' wealth unjustly fill their bellies with fire. | terra: Those who consume orphan property unjustly are in fact consuming fire, exposing what the descending, taking hand does to itself.
luna: After describing a substantial gift to a wife, this ayah forbids taking any of it back; it directly bounds the section's branch of reaching for what is not one's right.
luna: This neighbor gives the reason for the rule in 4:20: the spouses have been intimate and taken a solemn covenant from one another, placing a moral boundary on reclaiming a gift.

luna: The section's dark ع ط و branch is taking what one has no right to; this command forbids consuming one another's wealth wrongfully and allows trade by mutual consent. | terra: Property may not be consumed wrongfully; only trade by mutual consent is allowed, setting consent as the boundary between exchange and the section’s taking of what is not one’s right.
terra: The miserly command others to miserliness and conceal what God gave them from His bounty, opposing both the open hand and the command to make divine favor known.
terra: After naming revelation and teaching given to the Prophet, the ayah says God’s favor upon him is immense, supplying concrete content for speaking of his Lord’s favor.

luna: The section forbids overpowering an orphan; this ruling calls for justice toward orphan girls and children, including those whose prescribed rights might be withheld. | terra: The people ask for a ruling about women and orphan girls whose prescribed due they do not give, so سؤال and the withholding hand converge around the orphan’s right.
terra: The command to remember God’s favor is joined to remembering the covenant they voiced, linking received niʿma with spoken acknowledgment.
terra: A commanded remembrance of God’s favor recounts enemies stretching out their hands and God restraining them, joining niʿma to the prevention of a wrongful reaching hand.

luna: The section connects هدى with a gift; this ayah says God guides those who seek His pleasure by the Book from darkness to light and to paths of peace, making guidance a received benefit with a destination.
terra: Moses tells his people to remember God’s favor in making prophets and rulers among them and giving them what others had not received.
terra: Abel says that even if his brother stretches a hand to kill him, he will not stretch his own hand back, contrasting the wrongful reaching hand with deliberate restraint.
luna: The section's ع ط و note includes taking what is not rightfully yours; the theft ruling treats unlawful taking as a hand-action with a legal boundary.

luna: The section pictures giving with an open hand; this ayah rejects the claim that God's hand is bound and says His hands are extended and He spends as He wills (يداه مبسوطتان ينفق كيف يشاء), a direct reversal of withholding. | terra: The charge that God’s hand is bound is answered with “His two hands are outspread” (يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ) and He spends as He wills, making the open divine hand explicit.
luna: The disciples ask Jesus whether his Lord can send down a table from heaven; this begins a passage in which petitioners seek a gift from above, close to the section's ask-and-give movement.
luna: The disciples explain in 5:112 that they want to eat from the table and reassure their hearts; their stated need makes the requested heavenly gift more than a spectacle.
luna: Jesus asks for the table as a feast and sign and says “provide for us”; this neighbor gives the heavenly gift a communal and provisionary purpose.
luna: God answers the request in 5:112–114 by promising to send the table down, then warns those who disbelieve afterward; the grant from above carries a boundary of responsibility.

luna: The section glosses قهر as dominance and taking from above; here God is القاهر فوق عباده, a sovereign use of the same above/dominance image that contrasts with human oppression of an orphan. | terra: God is “the Overpowering above His servants” (ٱلْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ), matching the dictionary’s qahr from above while marking the boundary between divine sovereignty and a human overpowering an orphan.

luna: The same قاهر فوق عباده formula appears before God's messengers take each person at death; its context makes the section's “from above” power divine custody, unlike the forbidden human grasp. | terra: The repeated title “the Overpowering above His servants” precedes the taking of souls by messengers, again reserving legitimate qahr from above to God.

luna: After listing gardens, crops, and fruit, this ayah commands people to give its due on harvest day and not waste (آتوا حقه يوم حصاده ولا تسرفوا), joining provision to measured giving. | terra: At harvest, people must give the crop’s due yet not waste, joining a recipient’s right to a measured rather than limitless opening of the hand.

luna: The section forbids overpowering an orphan; this command forbids approaching the orphan's property except in the best way until maturity, protecting what the hand might take. | terra: Approaching an orphan’s property is forbidden except in the best manner until maturity, sharply limiting the guardian’s upper hand.
luna: The saved people say الحمد لله الذي هدانا لهذا; their spoken praise for God's guidance concretely joins the section's guided recipient to its command to speak of the Lord's favor.
terra: Salih tells Thamud to let God’s she-camel eat on God’s earth and not touch her with harm, supplying the protected freedom behind 7:77’s violation.
terra: Thamud hamstring the she-camel and defiantly demand punishment, another telling of the very act performed by the reaching companion in 54:29.
luna: Pharaoh's people claim إنا فوقهم قاهرون over the Israelites; this boast stages the abusive domination from above that the section forbids toward a vulnerable orphan.
terra: Those who criticize the distribution are satisfied if “they are given” (أُعْطُوا) and angry if not; it is a corrupt mirror of the Lord giving until the Prophet is satisfied.

terra: The proper response to distribution is satisfaction with what God and His messenger gave and hope that God “will give us” from His bounty, closely matching gift followed by contentment in 93:5 and correcting 9:58.

luna: This ayah names the recipients of obligatory charity, including the poor, needy, debtors, and stranded traveler; it supplies a concrete distribution setting for the section's asker and vulnerable recipients.
terra: Hypocrites command wrong, forbid right, and “close their hands” (يَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ), bodily reversing the open giving hand.

luna: This begins the passage completed in 9:76: people promise to give charity if God grants them bounty, making their request and intended return explicit. | terra: A person vows that if God gives from His bounty he will give charity and become righteous, explicitly promising that the receiving hand will become a giving hand.

luna: It completes 9:75: after God gives them from His bounty, they withhold and turn away, a direct reversal of the open hand and the sâ'il's hope. | terra: Once God gives the promised bounty, the recipient becomes stingy and turns away, breaking the passage of a gift through one hand to another.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to take charity from believers’ wealth and pray for them; this human taking hand and consoling speech lead directly to God taking charities in 9:104.
terra: God “takes the charities” (يَأْخُذُ ٱلصَّدَقَٰتِ), reversing the ordinary direction of giving as the divine hand above receives what the human hand offers.
terra: God purchases believers’ lives and wealth in exchange for the Garden and calls this covenant a sale, making the section’s “exchange between hands” an explicit transaction.
terra: People are told to rejoice in God’s bounty and mercy because it is better than what they accumulate, locating satisfaction in the divine gift rather than in hoarding.
terra: Salih similarly calls her God’s she-camel, lets her feed, and forbids harmful touch, defining what the taking hand had no right to seize.
terra: After they hamstring her, Salih announces their three-day respite, carrying the wrongful reach into its promised consequence.
luna: This ayah sets the people of the Fire in painful permanence; its neighbor 11:108 names the contrasting Paradise gift as عطاء غير مجذوذ, clarifying what “unsevered gift” answers.

luna: The section's root note for عطو meets the afterlife's عطاء غير مجذوذ, a gift “unsevered”; it makes the promised giving endure. | terra: The people made happy receive “a gift uncut” (عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ), clarifying how divine giving can remain rather than pass away.
terra: Yusuf contrasts many divided lords with “God, the One, the Overpowering”; the title locates qahr in undivided divine authority rather than human mastery of the weak.
terra: Joseph’s brothers arrive in hardship with poor merchandise and ask him to give full measure and charity, staging needy petitioners before a powerful hand able to fill theirs.
terra: After affirming God as creator of everything, the ayah names Him the One, the Overpowering, grounding qahr in universal creation rather than social power.
luna: The section sets the Hereafter as better than the first life; this ayah says God expands or restricts provision and contrasts rejoicing in this life with its small share against the Hereafter.
terra: Moses is told to remind his people of God’s favor in rescuing them from Pharaoh, another explicit movement from a saving divine act to verbal remembrance.

luna: The section ends with telling God's نعمة; this promise says gratitude for a favor brings increase, connecting acknowledgment with further giving. | terra: After the reminder of divine favor, God promises increase for gratitude and punishment for ingratitude, stating how the recipient’s acknowledgment meets the continuing gift.

luna: The section joins the asker, God's giving, and His نعمة; here God gives what people سألتموه and His نعمة cannot be counted, placing request, answer, and unmeasurable favor together. | terra: God gives from all that people ask of Him, then His favor proves uncountable; asking, fulfilled need, giving, and niʿma occur in one movement.
terra: All creation emerges before God, the One, the Overpowering, placing qahr in the final leveling where no human upper hand remains.
terra: “We have given you” the seven repeated verses and the great Qur’an is another completed divine grant addressed directly to the Prophet.
luna: The section's gazelle reaches up for leaves; this ayah mentions trees in which people pasture their animals, a broader grazing scene that recalls the animal reaching for food.

luna: The section calls نعمة a hand and favor; this ayah says that if people tried to count God's نعمة they could not number them, like 14:34's uncountable blessing. | terra: God’s favors cannot be counted, matching 14:34 and explaining why the commanded telling of favor cannot exhaust the gift.
terra: Every favor people possess is from God, and distress makes them cry to Him, joining the origin of the gift to the supplicant’s upward appeal.

luna: This ayah speaks of provision and God's نعمة, then asks whether people deny His favor; its picture of unequal provision and what is held back by right hands concretizes the section's hand-and-bounty link. | terra: People favored with greater provision refuse to hand it over so that those under their authority might share equally, and the ayah names this refusal a denial of God’s favor.
terra: People recognize God’s favor and then deny it, the direct failure of acknowledgment against which the command to speak of the Lord’s favor stands.

luna: The section tells the Prophet to speak of the Lord's نعمة; this command to eat God's provision and be grateful for His favor supplies a direct response to receiving. | terra: People must eat the good lawful provision God gave and thank His favor, connecting the received thing to verbal acknowledgment.
terra: Abraham is grateful for God’s favors, and God chooses and guides him, bringing favor and guidance together as the recipient’s gratitude answers the gift.

luna: The section names عطاء as a gift; this ayah calls provision for both groups عطاء ربك and says it is not withheld, showing the breadth of that divine giving. | terra: God extends provision to both worldly-seeking groups and says the Lord’s gift (عَطَآءُ رَبِّكَ) is not barred, displaying the reach of the giving hand.

luna: This command says to give relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due; it gives the section's reaching hand a concrete list of people to serve. | terra: The relative, needy person, and traveler must be given their due without squandering, supplying the right and recipients whose measured delivery continues through 17:29.

luna: The neighbor to the gift command in 17:26 calls spendthrifts brothers of devils; it bounds generosity against waste, like the section's warning against opening the hand fully. | terra: Calling squanderers brothers of devils explains one forbidden extreme before 17:29 measures the hand between closure and total extension.

luna: If one must turn away from the needy because one seeks mercy from the Lord, this neighbor commands a gentle word; it directly answers the section's ban on rebuking the asker. | terra: If one must turn away while awaiting provision from God, one must still speak gently; the unavailable gift is replaced by a fitting word rather than rebuffing the asker.

luna: The section's hand passes or receives a gift; this command says not to bind one's hand to one's neck or open it fully (ولا تبسطها كل البسط), giving the image a measure between withholding and excess. | terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor spread to its furthest extent, giving the section’s open hand an explicit measure and boundary.

luna: Following the hand measure in 17:29, this ayah says the Lord expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it; the neighbor turns the human rule of measured giving toward God's provision. | terra: The Lord expands and restricts provision with knowledge, returning the human hand measured in 17:29 to the divine hand that determines its means.

luna: The command not to approach an orphan's property except in the best way echoes the section's ban on taking from the vulnerable and extends it to keeping the covenant. | terra: The same ban on approaching orphan property except beneficially lasts until maturity, and the covenant must be fulfilled.
luna: The section says the Hereafter is better than the first life; this ayah contrasts worldly wealth and children with lasting good works, a related but less direct account of what remains.
terra: Moses and his companion ask a town’s people for food and are refused hospitality, a narrative instance of petitioners being rebuffed.

luna: The section protects the orphan against a hand that seizes; Moses learns that the wall was repaired to preserve the treasure of two orphan boys until they grew, an act of protection from above. | terra: A wall conceals treasure for two orphan boys until maturity, while God protects their due through an unseen act of mercy rather than allowing a stronger hand to seize it.
terra: The messenger tells Mary he has been sent by her Lord to grant her a pure boy, presenting a divine gift as something brought to its recipient by a messenger.
terra: God first draws attention to what Moses holds in his right hand, locating in the hand the staff whose leaf-giving use is explained in 20:18.
terra: Moses’ staff is held to beat foliage down for his sheep; the hand, tree, leaf, and feeding animal give a close Quranic counterpart to the dictionary’s animal reaching up for leaves.
terra: God tells Moses, “You have been granted your request” (أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ), exactly enacting the source dictionary’s sense of meeting an asker’s need.

luna: The section's ع ط و note derives giving from reaching by hand; Moses says God “gave each thing its creation, then guided it” (أعطى … هدى), making guidance follow the gift of a fitting nature. | terra: God “gave each thing its creation, then guided” (أَعْطَىٰ ... ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ), reproducing the section’s sequence of the giving hand and the guidance-gift.
terra: Sacrificial camels are provision from God from which people must eat and feed both the contented poor and the one who asks, pairing divine gift with two kinds of receiving need.
terra: People of bounty and means must not swear to stop giving relatives, the needy, and emigrants, so pardon reopens a hand that grievance had closed.

luna: The section's Lord gives and human hands transfer; this command tells believers to give enslaved people from God's wealth that He has given them. | terra: Those seeking emancipation contracts must be given from the wealth God gave the believers, so an initial divine gift must pass onward to release a dependent person.

luna: The section's hand should not be wholly closed or flung open; this ayah describes the faithful as spending neither extravagantly nor stingily, but in a middle course. | terra: The servants’ spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but a measured middle, paralleling the bounded opening of the hand in 17:29.
terra: Pharaoh calls Moses’ upbringing a favor while suppressing Israel; Moses’ reply exposes a “favor” recounted by an oppressor as a claim of ownership.
terra: Salih states that the she-camel has her drink and the people theirs on an appointed day, specifying the right violated by the later hand.
terra: They are forbidden to touch her with harm, stating the boundary immediately before they cross it.
terra: They hamstring her and become regretful, repeating the dark reaching-and-taking scene with its inward consequence.
luna: After recognizing the ant's speech, Solomon asks God to enable him to thank His نعمة; this makes the section's received favor lead to words addressed back to its giver.

luna: The section's ه د ي note links guidance with a gift; the Queen says she will send a هدية, making that root's material gift sense concrete. | terra: The queen sends a هَدِيَّة and waits to see what the messengers return with, staging the source dictionary’s gift carried from one friendly hand to another.

luna: After the Queen's هدية in 27:35, Solomon asks if they supply him wealth and says what God آتاني is better than theirs; his answer separates a human gift from God's greater grant. | terra: Solomon contrasts the envoys’ gift with what God has given him and says they rejoice in their gift; هَدِيَّتِكُمْ meets divine giving and tests whether a hand-to-hand offering is truly enriching.
terra: After rejecting the gift, Solomon sends it back and warns that overpowering armies would expel its senders humbled, showing the gift scene turning toward power from above.
luna: Solomon asks which member of his assembly will bring the Queen's throne; this starts a concrete ask-and-transfer scene that the following ayat complete.
luna: The jinn offers to bring the throne before Solomon rises; his spoken offer is the next step in the transfer requested in 27:38.
luna: The throne is placed before Solomon, who calls it فضل ربي and says the gift tests gratitude; the transfer ends in the section's pattern of receiving God's favor and speaking of it.
luna: After the throne arrives in 27:40, Solomon disguises it to test whether the Queen is guided; the passage brings the section's gift and هدى strands together in one scene.

luna: The response recognizes the throne and says knowledge had been given before it; this completes the test begun in 27:41 and places received knowledge beside a delivered object. The speaker of the final clause is uncertain in my recollection.

luna: Moses asks God for whatever خير He sends down because he is in need; the section's asker becomes a prayerful recipient awaiting provision. | terra: Moses names himself needy for any khayr God sends down; the supplicant below awaits good as a gift descending from the divine hand.

luna: This neighbor answers Moses' need in 28:24: one of the women invites him to her father to be paid for watering their flock, turning a request for خير into a human exchange. | terra: Immediately after Moses voices need for any good sent down, a woman comes with an invitation to receive a reward for watering, beginning the concrete answer to his open-handed prayer.
luna: The section's ه د ي note draws a gift sense from guidance; this ayah says the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves, but God guides whom He wills, locating that guidance with the giver.

luna: This command tells the addressee to give a relative, poor person, and traveler their due; it turns the section's open hand into directed generosity. | terra: The relative, needy person, and traveler must be given their right, making the transfer a due owed to the receiving hand rather than optional largesse.
terra: A gift intended to grow in other people’s wealth does not grow with God, whereas alms seeking God’s face multiply; the recipient and purpose determine what a transfer becomes.
terra: God has lavished favors both outward and inward, extending the section’s visible hand-gift to provision that remains hidden.
terra: Believers must remember God’s favor when unseen forces drove off the armies, so an invisible protecting hand becomes something recounted.
terra: The man is described as one whom God favored and the Prophet also favored, showing divine favor passing through a human relationship rather than ending with its first recipient.

luna: The section's gifts pass between hands; here God promises to replace what people spend, naming Him the best provider and completing the transfer with return. | terra: Whatever believers spend, God replaces it; the giving hand is itself supplied and answered by the supreme Provider.
luna: The section shows a hand giving and a hand that may hold; here what God opens of mercy no one can withhold, and what He withholds no one can send after, making Him the final giver and holder.
terra: People are commanded to remember God’s favor and asked whether any creator besides God provides for them, fastening the spoken favor to its sole giving source.
terra: All people are the needy ones toward God while God is self-sufficient, identifying every apparently giving human hand as fundamentally a receiving hand.
luna: This ayah joins reciting God's book, prayer, and spending from His provision privately and publicly, connecting the section's spoken mention of favor to the hand that gives.
luna: It completes the giving passage in 35:29: God pays the givers fully and increases them from His bounty, so the human gift is followed by divine return.

luna: Solomon asks God to forgive him and grant him a kingdom; this is the request that leads to the grant and choice over giving or holding in 38:39. | terra: Solomon asks his Lord to grant him an incomparable kingdom, supplying the request whose answer is later handed to him as “Our gift” in 38:39.
luna: God answers Solomon's request in 38:35 by subjecting the wind to him; it names a concrete part of the kingdom later called God's عطاؤنا in 38:39.

luna: Sulayman calls his grant هذا عطاؤنا and may give or hold it (أمسك); the same giving root makes visible a recipient's choice over what has been entrusted to him. | terra: “This is Our gift” (هَٰذَا عَطَآؤُنَا) leaves Solomon free to give or withhold, explicitly passing the giver’s hand into a human hand.
terra: The messenger declares no deity but God, the One, the Overpowering, making qahr part of exclusive divinity rather than a license for human domination.
terra: The One, the Overpowering is above the imagined choice of offspring, again attaching the root to God’s incomparable sovereignty.

luna: The ayah depicts the whole earth in God's قبضته and the heavens folded in His right hand; it gives a cosmic counterpart to the section's qahr as taking from above, while distinguishing divine sovereignty from human abuse.
terra: On the day when nothing is hidden, dominion belongs to God, the One, the Overpowering; every temporary human upper hand has disappeared.
luna: The section's generous hand still gives according to need; here God says He would let provision overflow if He did, but sends it down by measure, explaining restraint as deliberate measure.
luna: The section's خير of the Hereafter is set against gifts in this life; here what people are given is only its enjoyment, while what is with God is خير وأبقى.
terra: God grants female children to whom He wills and male children to whom He wills, presenting life itself as a discretionary gift from His hand.
terra: He joins sons and daughters or makes whom He wills barren, completing 42:49’s picture of giving with a boundary no human hand controls.
luna: The section's mihda is a platter that carries a gift; this scene has gold platters and cups carried around in Paradise, a plausible but uncertain parallel in serving vessels.
terra: If God were to demand all wealth and press people, they would become stingy and expose resentment; the ayah explains the measured divine demand before 47:38 calls them to spend.
terra: When called to spend, some withhold; the ayah answers that the withholder harms only himself because God is rich and humans are needy.

luna: The ayah says God's hand is above the believers' hands as they pledge allegiance; this is a covenantal hand relation rather than a material transfer, but it places human hands under divine authority. | terra: In the pledge, “God’s hand is above their hands” (يَدُ ٱللَّهِ فَوْقَ أَيْدِيهِمْ); a covenantal hand-to-hand act makes palpable the section’s meeting between the hand above and hands below.
terra: People count their submission as a favor to the Prophet, but God says His favor is that He guided them; niʿma/minna, telling, and guidance are disentangled in one correction.

luna: The section's open-palmed سائل is not a nuisance: this ayah says there is a right in the believers' wealth for the سائل and the deprived. | terra: The asker and the deprived possess a right within the believers’ wealth, so the open palm is met as a rights-bearing hand rather than an intrusion.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to remind people, and the Lord’s favor is named as the reason he is neither soothsayer nor madman; his speech is grounded in received niʿma.
terra: The condemned person “gave a little and withheld” (أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًۭا وَأَكْدَىٰ), placing the root’s giving motion beside the hand that abruptly closes.
terra: God sends the she-camel as a trial and commands watchful patience, introducing the living object toward which the wrongful hand will reach in 54:29.
terra: Water is to be divided and each share attended in turn, establishing the she-camel’s allotted right before the seizure in 54:29.

luna: The section names taʿāṭī as taking what is not one's right; in the she-camel scene one man فتعاطى ثم عقر, so the shared root becomes a destructive reach. | terra: Thamud call their companion, who reaches out (فَتَعَاطَىٰ) and hamstrings the she-camel; the same root’s taking hand becomes seizure of what was not his by right.
luna: The section's سائل asks for a gift; this ayah widens the scene to all in heaven and earth يسأله, with God continually acting as the one turned to.

luna: Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over; the section's giver-recipient handoff is framed as passing on wealth first received from God. | terra: Believers must spend from that over which God made them successors, showing that the human giver first receives temporary custody from the divine giver.

luna: The section shows giving and receiving; this ayah asks who will lend God a goodly loan, which He multiplies, turning a human gift into a promised divine return. | terra: The one who lends God a good loan receives it multiplied and a noble reward, a hand-to-hand exchange in which the divine return surpasses the human gift.

luna: It pairs men and women who give charity with those who lend God a goodly loan, promising multiplication and a noble reward; the section's handoff is explicitly answered by God's return. | terra: Charitable men and women who lend God a good loan receive it multiplied, extending the hand-to-hand loan image to actual donors of charity.
terra: Those who are miserly and command others to miserliness are answered by God’s self-sufficiency, another communal spread of the closed-hand posture.

luna: The section's upward-giving hand belongs to God; this ayah says no one controls His فضل and that bounty is in His hand, a boundary against treating the gift as human property. | terra: The People of the Book are told that bounty is in God’s hand and He gives it as He wills, again locating provision in the divine hand rather than human control.

luna: This rule distributes communal wealth to kin, orphans, the poor, and travelers so it will not circulate only among the rich; it gives the section's open hand a social rule against hoarding. | terra: Fay is assigned to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so wealth does not merely circulate among the rich; “what the Messenger gives you, take” also makes distribution a commanded giving-and-taking act.
luna: The next ayah identifies the poor emigrants as people expelled from homes and property who seek God's bounty; it specifies vulnerable recipients within the distribution named in 59:7.

luna: This neighbor describes the Helpers welcoming and preferring the emigrants even while needy, and being protected from stinginess; it shows giving to the vulnerable at personal cost. | terra: The Helpers prefer others over themselves despite their own need, so a needy hand can still open and give rather than treating need as a reason to withhold.
terra: Enemies stretch their hands and tongues toward believers with evil, coupling hostile hand and hostile speech where the section joins beneficent hand and speech.
terra: At death a person asks for a short delay in order to give charity, making a would-be giver first an asker before the divine hand that controls time.

luna: The command to spend for one's own good is paired with protection from شح (stinginess); it makes the closed hand a spiritual danger, as in the section's contrast between giving and withholding. | terra: The command to spend for one’s own good is joined to protection from the soul’s stinginess, identifying the inner force that closes the hand.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, showing the giver becoming a receiver from the One to whom the gift was offered.
terra: Each person spends according to what God has given, and God promises ease after hardship; the human hand’s measure is set by the prior divine gift.
terra: The Lord’s favor is again invoked to reject the charge of madness against the Prophet, giving a specific divine benefit that his proclamation makes known.
terra: Ordinary man becomes withholding when good reaches him, directly opposing the people whose wealth contains the asker’s right in 70:24–25.

luna: The section's asker appears here as a defined claim: the faithful keep a known حق in their wealth, which 70:25 identifies for the asker and deprived. | terra: Their wealth contains “a known right,” establishing that the giver’s transfer in 70:25 is an obligation with a measure, not arbitrary generosity.

luna: This neighbor specifies the right named in 70:24 as belonging to the سائل and the deprived, giving the section's asker a place in the giver's wealth. | terra: The known right belongs “to the asker and the deprived” (لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ), repeating the pairing in 51:19 and including the need that remains unspoken.
terra: The command not to confer a favor in order to get more prevents the gift from becoming a self-enriching claim over the recipient.

luna: The section names the orphan and the asker among vulnerable recipients; here the righteous give food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite loving it. | terra: The righteous give food they love to the needy person, orphan, and captive, staging the transfer to two recipients central to the section.

luna: This neighbor explains the feeding in 76:8: the givers seek God's face and desire neither repayment nor thanks, making the gift free of a claim on its recipient. | terra: They seek neither repayment nor thanks from those they feed, keeping the gift from becoming a hand-to-hand bargain for praise.

luna: After the feeding and pure intention in 76:8–9, God protects the givers from that day's evil and gives them radiance and joy; this completes the passage with a return that answers the section's promised satisfaction.
terra: The frown and turning away supply the bodily opposite of receiving a vulnerable petitioner without rebuke.
terra: The blind man’s arrival identifies the vulnerable person from whom the response in 80:1 turned away.
terra: The other side of the episode is the person who comes striving toward the Prophet, giving direction and effort to the petitioner’s approach.
terra: His fear makes clear the sincere need behind that approach rather than a claim on worldly rank.
terra: Being distracted from that sincere visitor completes the cautionary scene opposite the command not to rebuff the asker.

luna: The section's lexical example is an animal reaching for leaves; this ayah names provision for people and their livestock after pasture, a broad animal-feeding parallel without the reaching gesture.
luna: The section's claim that the Hereafter is better than the first life is restated as “the Hereafter is better and more enduring” (والآخرة خير وأبقى), extending the contrast to permanence.

luna: The section forbids humiliating the orphan; this rebuke says people fail to honor (لا تكرمون) the orphan, naming the social reversal of that command. | terra: “You do not honor the orphan” names the social posture opposite the prohibition against overpowering the orphan.

luna: The same rebuke continues from 89:17: people do not urge one another to feed the poor, extending orphan neglect into refusal to provide. | terra: The same people do not urge one another to feed the needy, showing a community that keeps every giving hand closed.

luna: The rebuke continues to devouring inheritance greedily; this gives a concrete picture of the unjust hand the section warns against. | terra: They devour inheritance voraciously, continuing the orphan context with the image of a stronger party consuming another’s due.
luna: The closing charge of this sequence is intense love of wealth; beside the orphan's neglected claim in 89:17–19, it shows what the grasping hand serves.

luna: The section's care for a vulnerable recipient is staged as feeding during famine; the next verses specify an orphan near at hand and then a destitute person. | terra: “Feeding on a day of hunger” supplies the concrete act whose receiving figures are named in the next two ayat.

luna: This neighbor specifies one recipient of the famine feeding in 90:14 as an orphan who is a close relative. | terra: The first recipient of that feeding is an orphan of kin, directly answering the section’s demand that the stronger hand protect the orphan.

luna: This neighbor adds the poor person in the dust to the famine scene begun in 90:14, showing another recipient of the extended hand. | terra: The second recipient is a destitute person in the dust, giving bodily form to the deprived person whose need may or may not be voiced.
terra: God’s messenger warns them concerning “God’s she-camel and her drink,” again naming both the protected creature and her right.
terra: They deny the messenger and hamstring her, after which their Lord crushes them for the sin; the hand that overpowered the vulnerable meets overpowering judgment.

luna: This is the section's stated example of the giver: the one who أعطى and is mindful. It places human giving alongside the Lord's gift in 93:5. | terra: The one who “gives and is mindful” (أَعْطَىٰ وَٱتَّقَىٰ) is the praised human giving hand immediately before this surah.
terra: God promises to ease the giver of 92:5 toward ease, showing the divine return that follows the praised human gift.

luna: The section praises the one who gives; the paired warning begins with whoever withholds (بخل) and thinks himself self-sufficient, the reversed hand in the previous surah. | terra: The one who is stingy and imagines himself self-sufficient is the closed-hand reversal of the giver in 92:5.
terra: Being eased toward hardship is the answering outcome of the withholding posture begun in 92:8.
luna: The section's giver transfers a gift; here a God-fearing person يوتي ماله to purify himself, making human giving a response to the divine gift.
luna: The section's grant ends with satisfaction (فترضى); at the end of the giving passage begun in 92:18, the giver too “will be satisfied” (ولسوف يرضى), linking giving with contentment.

luna: The section tells the addressee not to qahr the orphan; this ayah exposes the denier of judgment as one who يدع اليتيم, driving the orphan away. | terra: The denier is the one who violently repels the orphan, an enacted opposite of “do not overpower the orphan.”
terra: He does not urge feeding the needy, extending the repulsed orphan scene into refusal to mobilize any giving hand.

luna: The section's ع ط و root is used directly in أعطيناك: God gives the Prophet al-Kawthar, an explicit instance of the promised hand reaching its recipient. | terra: “We have given you al-Kawthar” (أَعْطَيْنَٰكَ ٱلْكَوْثَرَ) is the completed divine gift to the same prophetic addressee promised satisfaction in 93:5.
